text: Encryption comes in two real flavors, and almost every secure system you use combines them. Symmetric encryption uses one shared key. Asymmetric encryption uses a linked pair of keys. Each solves a different problem, and understanding both is what makes HTTPS, the padlock in your browser, actually make sense.

Symmetric encryption, like AES, uses a single shared key to both encrypt and decrypt. Whoever holds that key can lock the data, and the same key unlocks it. It's computationally cheap, which is why it's fast enough to encrypt gigabytes of disk or a live video stream. But it has one hard problem: both sides need the exact same key before they can talk securely, and sending that key in plain text over a network an attacker might be watching defeats the entire point.

Asymmetric encryption, like RSA, solves that by using two mathematically linked keys instead of one. The public key can be shared with absolutely anyone — posted on a website, emailed, it doesn't matter. The private key never leaves its owner. Data locked with the public key can only be unlocked with the matching private key, so no secret ever has to travel in the open. The trade-off is speed — the math is far more expensive, so it's too slow for bulk data on its own.

TLS, the protocol behind HTTPS, uses both together. During the initial handshake, it uses asymmetric encryption just long enough to safely exchange a freshly generated symmetric session key. From that point on, both sides switch to fast symmetric encryption using that session key for every page, image, and request. Asymmetric solves the key-exchange problem once, at the start; symmetric does the actual heavy lifting for the rest of the connection.

That's how symmetric and asymmetric encryption work together in the real world. Next up: hashing, digital signatures, and the public key infrastructure that makes the trust chain behind HTTPS actually hold together.
